cultivar: Wild large-leaf tea trees, sometimes sold as Camellia sinensis var. dehungensis
processing: Closed leaf buds are picked and simply sun-dried with nothing else done. Slight oxidation during drying is why some sellers class it as a white pu-erh rather than a white tea.
harvest_season: Very early spring, before the buds open.
appearance_dry: Whole, tight, cone-shaped buds wrapped in scales, silvery to pale brown, and looking more like pine buds than like tea leaf.
appearance_liquor: Very pale, clear and sparkling, from straw to light gold.
appearance_wet: Plump scaled buds that swell slightly, in tan and pale green.
taste_profile: Light, clean and resinous, with pine, wood and a touch of earth, opening into floral and citrus notes when the water is hot enough.

brewing.notes: Unlike most white teas it needs hot water, 90 to 95 C, or it gives only an earthy, resinous cup. It also works gongfu style and is good chilled.

vintage_note: Sold mainly as the current spring collection, by year, from wild tree areas. It is often found in small batches at specialist shops. There is little documented aged market for it, though some keep it like raw pu-erh material.
description:
Ya Bao is one of the oddest things you can buy as tea: not leaves or tips but the tight, scaled buds of wild large-leaf trees in Yunnan, picked before they open. It looks like something from a pine tree, and that first impression is a fair guide to the cup.

The making could not be simpler. The buds are picked in early spring and sun-dried, and that is all. Because a little oxidation happens during drying, sellers differ on calling it white tea or white pu-erh.

The cup is pale, light and clean, with wood and pine at first and something floral or citrus underneath. People usually get it wrong by treating it as a delicate white tea. Cool water brings only the resin, so use it hot and give it time. It is also good chilled.

Most of what is sold comes through specialist importers, with wild purple types among them. Origin claims are mostly the seller's word, so ask what region and tree type it is. Try a Yue Guang Bai next for a very different take on Yunnan white.
history: Ya Bao is recognised as a Yunnan all-bud white tea, but little is documented about its origin. It reaches Western and Russian-speaking drinkers mainly through tea importers, and those sellers give different growing areas, such as Dehong. No reliable record of when or by whom it was first sold as a named tea is available.
